作为一款融合了塔可夫玩法的第一人称射击肉鸽游戏，可以说既没做好塔可夫的游戏体验，又没做好肉鸽游戏的重复可玩度。以至于现在的火湖是一款非常抽象的融合怪。 关于塔可夫玩法：塔可夫玩法讲究三个字“搜、打、撤”，即局内搜索，打怪撤离。然而局内的战利品少的可怜，有时候一章下来能有几个物品就谢天谢地，大部分都是食材。这就不得不提这游戏幽默的烹饪系统了。食物基本上是玩家回复的唯一手段，但是烹饪系统做的一坨。几乎所有的食物配方全凭玩家自己尝试，平均体验就是在锅前面倒腾半小时，然后打架几分钟。还得背着这些看似有用，实则在你没试出来配方前完全没用的食材满大街跑。尽管局内体验做成了一坨，他还是念念不忘死亡物品全部消失。人家这么做好歹有市场这种东西支持，死了花点钱从新买一套装备就能接着打。而这游戏的商店纯随机，你打十几小时才能拼出来一把像样的武器，有可能一局失误就送了。想在获得同样的武器，对不起，慢慢刷去吧，前提是能活着带出来并且在接下来完全不死。 关于肉鸽方面：游戏几乎没任何重复可玩度，唯一能让你重复打下去的动力也许就是能不能收集齐所有的武器和装备。差不多5-8小时就能体验完游戏全部的内容，剩下就是刷装备了。如果你不是收集党，那么游戏几乎没有任何动力让你重复去打，仅此而已。造成这一现象的根本原因是局内成长几乎为0，完全依赖局外成长。你这把带进副本的武器强弱，护甲好坏就基本决定了这一局的走向了。武器依赖熟练度和改装，也就意味着局内掉落的武器几乎没法用，所以局内的武器更多是以战利品的形式带出去，而非捡起来就用。这就导致最起码肉鸽游戏的随机性消失了，变成了千篇一律的刷副本。 我是很喜欢火湖的武器设计的，奔放又具有想象力。但如果火湖不对游戏本身的硬性问题进行调整，那终将成为一款食之无味弃之可惜的遗憾作品。至少做到让玩家打得爽，搜的开心。而不是用大量重复没意义的烹饪拖玩家战斗的节奏，用几乎没任何战利品房间的地图恶心玩家。
无敌好玩，蹲一波联机 完美解决了单机肉鸽不够刺激的问题 就是牛魔那个燃烧瓶的音效能不能改改，每次掏出来耳朵都聋了(⓿_⓿)

如看到这条评论的您所见，这并不是一款爽游，至少目前我认为不是。 首先是两个关卡间的难度差距太大。举一个例子。在第一张地图洞穴我们只需要面对拥有少量远程敌方单位，以及比较“脆弱的”敌方单位，这些怪物我们用简单强化过的枪械就能够轻松的应付。而第二张地图小镇拥有大量的远程单位，和一些难缠的较敏捷的近战单位，而且这些怪物的数值比上一张地图都普遍上升许多，这就不得不导致我们多刷几次一图，以获得护甲高的装备与武器经验，以提高容错率，如果运气好也许3次就够了，如果运气不好。。。。算了祝你好运。 其次是怪物设计与地图设计问题，其一我不明白为什么小怪有无敌时间，持续时间还那么长，而移动速度快的怪出现的那么多就算了，还伤害高血量厚。。。打这些玩意的时候，真是酣畅淋漓的赤石啊。 其二地图分支问题，在第四张地图地牢（树篱迷宫我按第3.5张算的）开始，每一张地图会出现分支，而分支的尽头无法通向道路主干，玩家只能以跑回分叉点的方式来重回道路。这样设计我想不到除了浪费时间还有什么用处，当然如果分叉的空缺内容是制作组的更新计划，那这是极好的。 其三，地图六森林给我一种廉价恐怖游戏的错觉，能够让我感到惊讶的只有树木倒下时像路边野狗跑出的中型乌鸦，这张图给我的其它感觉只能说是又臭又长。第九张图沙漠，这位更是重量级，意义不明，只会恶心到玩家的能见度降低滤镜，和那阴间怪，我只能说这关的目的只是为了恶心到我那制作组，你成功了。。。还有这张图的遗迹，经常因为能见度低看不见，或是因此浪费很多时间，史！！！ 然后，其一，就是魔油削弱的问题，我的评价是，这是一个射击爽游，为了流派多样性，与其削弱一个流派，不如加强另一套流派，我是近期入坑没经历太多，就不再多评价了。其二，烹饪系统，菜谱太多了也太杂了，菜品的作用，效果，售价都不是很合理或者说远不如制作成本。 最后，说说优点吧。极其抽象的神经枪械总会逗笑你，当你拿着你的满改神人枪械去开无双，或者1秒清空boss血槽时这种快乐会加倍。文案中或多或少的黑色幽默也是不得不品的一环。魔油，卷轴，饰品（爆的有点少，遗迹不想刷），装备4者组合，嗯，十分自由，按寻思这套能行（我们仍未知道制作组有多少bug要修）。 总之无爽游有很多，超越它的也很多，但当期同赛道我只看到他一个，嗯，未来可期（别蒸蒸日上）。没买的兄弟先别急，先放愿望单吧，没事看看更了啥，更了点好活再说。现在买也挺好，当支援未来了嘛（别给勾槽的制作组饿死了，我得等到什么时候玩到同类游戏）。

The art and the ideas are great, the guns are many and feel different between each other, but there are several problems. tl;dr: - problems with steam deck despite being listed as verified - too little variety for a roguelike - (this is subjective) I would like more meta-progress/unlocks - EDIT: impossible to save during a run or go back at the end of an area Long version: The game is listed as verified on Steam Deck, so I would have expected to have no problems playing it there. It is one of the reason I bought the game in the first place. Instead, the crafting menu is quite messy when used on deck. The tooltip menus cover the options, pressing Y to craft would also remove stuff from the inventory. It does not make the game unplayable, but given that the game relies on few well-developed mechanics, and one of them is crafting, this was really disappointing. I understand it's still early access, but then it should not be "verified". Hopefully it will be fixed in the final version. I like the graphic style of the game and the rooms of the levels are really nice, except it feels there are only very few of them for each biome. In every run I have found the same room layout over and over and over. Given that you are supposed to play the same environment over and over, this becomes a problem very soon. Same thing applies to enemies. For context, I have played little less than 10 hours, reaching the Dungeon (but not finishing it). By the time I had finished a biome, I felt I had seen everything there was to see there and I was actually relieve it was over.. Which would be okay in a plot-oriented game, but in a roguelike it's a major flaw. This is also connected to the very subjective desire for more meta-progression or unlocks. I totally understand that the devs wanted to go in a more "traditional" direction, with a punishing game that is closer to the original rogue than the more recent takes on the genre. So maybe I am simply not their target. While the stamp system allows to perform small upgrades on the church, I feel they have a very niche impact, and many of them are just "exibition" slots for weapons or whatever. It feels like any death would bring you back from where you started, and you have to go through a large part of the game to recover from that loss. And in the same way I don't love games where you have to grind over and over to pass a boss, I don't love games where you have to grind over and over to recover from failure, I see them as two versions of the same thing. And given the limited variety of content inside biomes, the perspective of having to go through all that again in case I fail feels like a chore. I am not asking for permanent power-ups as in Hades or similar, but for example progression of shops as in Duckov, so that you don't have to grind levels over and over, but you can buy part of your losses. But once again, this last point is very subjective, and it may go openly against the vision of the game. EDIT: I have just discovered that (1) you can not save during a run and (2) you can not go back to the curch at the end of a zone (except mines). This means that if in any moment you need/want to stop playing you must use your medallion, which works only if you have reached the middle of a level or was previously charged. I really can not fathom the motivation of such decisions. The first one may have technical motivation, but that honestly feel weird. The second one I really can not understand why any dev would impose such a limitation
It's a good game now and has high potential moving forward-- assuming the devs don't sell out. There's a lot more to this game than I thought.

Not very good or interesting at all. Sulfur gives you a huge amount of cool stuff to experiment with and then actively discourages you from doing so, by locking upgrades onto items. These items are extremely expensive Gameplay is extremely easy, with the difficulty being entirely centred around losing items upon death. You spend an hour trudging through dreary fights and then lose everything if you make a mistake. Yes this is what extraction shooters are but most of them give you at least some level of risk/reward tradeoffs, active decision making and challenges. Sulfur is just completely linear, it puts enemies in front of you and you shoot them while they run at you and you have no real choice in approach, bar maybe if you use gun 1 or gun 2. Enemy AI is extremely basic, they walk at you and fire their guns. Nothing wrong with that except the game is pitching itself as this high-octane fightfest and it isn't. I have no idea why the game is calling itself a roguelike, I didn't see any roguelike elements in my time playing. I don't think that randomised loot drops qualify that tag. The game is a linear extraction shooter with some platforming elements. If you're not an extraction shooter guy then don't buy this game because it isn't all these other things it's pretending to be. If you are an extraction shooter guy, I still think that, frankly, you can do better than this linear offering. Particularly egregious is its recipe system. The game has literally hundreds of recipes (overwhelmingly for health items), but locating these recipes is almost impossible - we're talking one might drop every couple of hours. So right now, either use the wiki (which is exceptionally slow when you're looking up ten items at a time to see what recipes they have) or just play with no healing items. It's just straight up bad game design. I just basically feel lied to. 游戏整体难度适中。虽说死亡会失去所有物品，但游戏地图资源给的十分慷慨，随便跑个刀就又能是条好汉。 游戏的改枪系统是最让我惊喜的，它不仅仅是简单的对枪加装配件，而是在这个基础上使用名为魔油的道具对枪械进行彻底的改装。你可以将一把枪改为n连发，又或是让子弹到处飞溅形成半径为20米的子弹结界（bushi）。在游戏中我就将一把冲锋枪改成了一把拥有超大弹夹超绝射速的喷子虽然它后座大的飞起，并杀穿了所有地图。不止这些，游戏中的枪械拥有伤害，射速，后坐力，散步，子弹类型等属性，而这些属性都是可以通过魔油改装的，这赋予改枪系统深度，让每个玩家都有机会改出属于自己的枪。在这基础上游戏有着相当优秀的射击手感，让玩家改的爽，射的爽！ 游戏内的料理系统也值得说道。料理系统并是配方合成，它更像塞尔达中的料理系统，玩家无法提前知道料理的结果，需要探索特定的食材组合并得到料理，同时它也会记录过往的合成结果减少玩家记忆的压力。当我突发其实将一些食材组合起来并真的收获了一道料理，那种惊喜感是配方合成无法带给我的体验。但是部分料理的合成路径复杂且角度刁钻让人难以想到，作者解决这个问题的方法简单粗暴，就是在商店售卖食谱书，这确实解决了问题，但是也丧失了探索的过程。[b]我个人认为可以通过线索提示食谱，如写有料理特征的描述的纸条，又或是将食谱加入NPC的委托奖励中[/b]，因为现版本中NPC委托的奖励实在是有点单薄，完成一次NPC的委托我往往需要放弃其他的补给品并耗费大量的时间但换来的只是短期无法获得收益的邮票，将食谱加入委托奖励可以说是一举两得。 美中不足的是，游戏的地图设计略显平庸。游戏的地图采用程序化生成整体构造并结合预制房间，这使得刚开始探索地图的几轮，每一轮的探索体验都能略有不同，但随着探索次数的增加都会感到地图的重复度高。同时房间设计缺乏记忆点，点名批评森林和沙漠这两张地图，走到哪都一个样子，我得通过击杀敌人的血迹来判断是否探索过一块区域。 最后关于敌人，由于前文提到的劲霸强的冲锋喷子，几乎没有敌人给我带来过威胁，只有森林的大乌鸦给我留下了深刻印象（咬牙），读指令挡子弹属实恶心。除此之外，敌人的生成逻辑有待改进，经常碰到在狭小的环境生成了大量的敌人，让人难以应付。

It's not exactly what it's internet marketing is selling it as. After 20 hours on and off between updates, I'd tell anyone to give this one a pass for now. The art, music, and theme are all excellent, the overall design of the game is great, but it just doesn't preform well in any of the gameplay aspects it's going for. Loot is sparse. Despite their being tons of guns and armor items to try out, 90% of the loot is healing items, and there's little to no options or opportunities to purchase weapons and armor from the hub/safezone. I've beaten each level several times, and there's still dozens of guns and armors I've never gotten to try; Good luck when an update comes out and they add new items, as the only way to experience them is grinding through an RNG pool on the same couple maps with high chest counts. The enemies are fine. Their designs are nice and they're varied. Early on it feels like the humans are just a reskin of the goblins, but past that they start to have unique traits like flying, blinding you, sneak attacks etc. They're a little bullet spongey on the recommended difficulty, and the AI is nothing to write home about, but overall they're not broken or buggy, and provide a challenge without being impossible. The game doesn't really have any roguelike/lite mechanics. There's no character progression or upgrades, just a stash of items you've made it home with, any of which you'll lose upon death. Depending on how runs go, this either leaves you with boxes full of mostly junk, or copies of the same weapons/armor you like and can find taking up the space. The quest system is also almost entirely based on RNG, with quests typically being "Find this one healing item out of 500" or "Bring X monster drop with a random drop%", and completing the quests only rewards you with more storage space (And rerolls for the shops, which will continue to sell nothing after each roll.) The biggest selling point for the game is it's gun customization. You can use up to 5 upgrades on each weapon to change it's characteristics drastically. In theory, this is the most entertaining aspect of the game; It's very satisfying to end up with 20-homing-rocket-per-shot shotgun, or find that perfect combo that clears a room/boss in a blink. But with the scarcity of loot, both weapons and upgrades, it becomes more frustrating to experiment with new guns/idea than fun, often times ending up with weapons that are notably worse after upgrading them than they were at base, unless you're following a guide or recreating a great one you've already used. I can imagine somebody picking up on the best min/max stats and strategies for each gun/type over time, but you'll still be left with the seemingly endless grind to acquire the specific upgrades you need to make a good build happen. All in all, the progression feels too hardcore for how cartoony/shallow the gameplay loop is. It'd be something I'd hop on every once in a while if I had easier options with experimenting with gun/gear builds, via some kind of gun/armor store that sells more than 0-1 weapons a run. They recently added a merchant that lets you re-purchase guns you've max ranked (For a ludicrous cost), which helps a little, but doesn't address the issue of the guns you can't find run after run, or the upgrades you need to make them playable. It's a 5/10, I'd keep an eye on it for future updates and full release, but I wouldn't really recommend it to it's audience in it's current state.

SULFUR has been one of my favorite indie shooters for quite a while now. It's a game that's able to mix this fantastical, spiritual world with basic concepts and explore them to the maximum depth a small studio can handle. The gameplay is fair, for the most part, the guns are quite unique while still filling their own niches, and the enemy variety is vastly better than most shooters. The story, while it may be a bit filled with holes and drowned in mystique, it still manages to be compelling enough to listen to characters and pay attention. It's well loved, received updates on a semi-consistent basis since launch, the end game could use a bit more fleshing out, and certain enemies could stand to be balanced differently (I hate enemies with invulnerability that make me wait in a game that seems to be designed around fast TTK); but overall its fun, it has a lot of crazy food, and characters that make me smile.

The game is interesting in concept and execution. The gunplay, gun variety, and movement feels satisfying. Enemy variety is unique and makes you think before attacking to a degree but overall is a fast-paced shooter. However, the story is a little lacking with not much being revealed about the main character (in a single run), and it kinda feels like the story was slightly tacked on as updates were being released. I enjoyed the environmental story telling of how each enemy type and background details unfolded from one area to the next. Like how the church people are searching the caves to look for lost souls to strip their flesh in order to "save their soul". How the masks being removed gets the zealots killed, and how the Witch's corruption had spread throughout the landscape. But in terms of the actual story... the ending felt very rushed. Waiting for the witch update to finally come out, the boss fight was pretty underwhelming. I am glad for a New Game+, but what's disappointing is that the game somewhat lacks challenge once you get certain weapons. Bosses and enemies become a complete joke with certain combos and the only thing keeping the player from deleting the gun that they made (which takes long to level up) is either to challenge themselves or to try new things. The strange thing is that the first act, the cave, felt more focused with a genuine level design concept of something thought out. The Cave not only has a more unique boss, but also has a mini-boss and reward with more levels. But the other areas never share the same thing, which sucks because I feel there could've been more variety with the design of the levels with unique one-off segments or challenges similar to a mini-boss room mid area. I'd like to see more unique rogue-lite elements added to levels with curses or blessings based on how deep you've gotten into the world, which a larger variety of melee weapons

No option to return to base after a boss Why isn't there an option after every completed level to simply say: "I'm done. I don't want to use my amulet. Just send me back to base after this boss." That would make farming much less frustrating. 3. Damage is wildly inconsistent The damage numbers in this game make no sense. One dog sometimes dies to a single .50 BMG round, while another survives three. It doesn't seem to matter where I shoot. If I see a damage number of 350, and a melee attack deals 70, shouldn't that be in total 420 damage? Why is the enemy still alive? I know the game has a limb damage system, but honestly, I don't think it fits a fantasy roguelite. Or what It may be. 4. Weapons and builds Most weapons feel underwhelming. You either: * Experiment with stats and hope your build works, * Look up an online guide, * Or accidentally ruin your build with a single potion. Then your five-slot build carries everything while the blood mechanic wipes your slots clean. Why can't we recover our potions? Like most of the game, builds feel random. I wish there was more consistency instead of hoping the right combination works. 5. Enemy design The enemies are one of the game's weakest points. Many have almost perfect aim the moment you stand still for a second. The crow section is by far my least favorite. Throwing 15 enemies at the player, with several ranged enemies shooting from far away while smaller enemies rush you, isn't challenging—it's just frustrating. Then the game expects you to loot everything while surviving the chaos. 6. Stats barely matter For a roguelite, you never really feel stronger. Defense doesn't seem to matter. Charisma feels pointless. Explosions destroy you regardless. Whether you have 10 Defense or 50 Defense, the result often feels the same. The only stat that consistently matters is sprint speed, because running away is usually the best strategy. 7. Quest system and money The inventory system is frustrating. Need more storage? Too bad. Items for upgrades are random, so if you want backup gear after dying, prepare to grind for hours. Money also becomes almost useless later in the game. Why can't I simply buy more storage space with my money? Instead I'm forced to grind stamps. 8. Experience grind Bosses barely give any experience. Leveling weapons takes far too long. The longer you stay in early levels to grind XP, the higher your chances of dying because of one small mistake. 9. Food system The food system is... fine. At one point I had an entire fridge full of pizza. But does the game really need over 500 recipes? Am I playing a cooking game or a shooter? 10. Gun customization For a game centered around guns, there are surprisingly few meaningful gun parts. Most upgrades are tiny stat boosts. Meanwhile, I have 20 different ways to cook an omelet. 11. Trinkets Trinkets are extremely rare, and many of them are disappointing. Examples: * 140% airborne damage... so I should jump around, lose accuracy, and take fall damage? * The Buddy relic barely does anything. * The 3x loot relic isn't always helpful. Sometimes I actually want lower-tier food items for quests or cooking. More loot doesn't always mean better loot. 12. Inspecting items The inspect feature feels unnecessary. It seems like development time that could have been spent elsewhere. 13. Melee weapons The katana is basically the only melee weapon worth using because of its sweeping attack. Everything else feels inferior. And honestly... this is supposed to be a gun game. 14. Elements Fire blocks enemy vision. Water barely does anything. Electricity can kill you. There are so many elemental items, yet most just sit in storage because they aren't worth using. 15. Stamp prices They're simply too expensive. 16. Enemy corpses block bullets After killing enemies, their bodies continue blocking bullets. This creates situations where your shots hit a corpse while melee enemies walk up behind it and hit you. This especially hurts automatic weapons, making single-fire weapons feel much stronger. 17. Soundtrack I turned the music off. Verry loopie my bro 18. Wiki dependency I found myself searching the wiki far too often. A game shouldn't require that much outside research just to understand its mechanics. # Overall Score 3/10 The concept is fantastic: a first-person roguelite shooter sounded like something I would absolutely love. Unfortunately, the execution falls short. Too many mechanics feel random instead of rewarding. Stats rarely feel meaningful, progression is grindy, inventory management is frustrating, and enemy encounters often rely on overwhelming the player rather than creating interesting challenges or be fun.
